description: We’re building LunarEnvelope, a global lunar landing-site navigator for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Our goal is to compare selected lunar locations and dates using NASA data, terrain context, and Sun/Earth visibility,while clearly showing sources, assumptions, and limitations. We’re looking for collaborators in coding, web development, lunar/geospatial science, data visualization, testing, design, and science communication. Beginners who enjoy learning and teamwork are welcome.
summary:
Lunaris is an interactive prototype for exploring the lunar environment and comparing potential lunar south-pole sites. It combines a 3D lunar globe, a south-polar elevation map, Sun and Earth geometry, terrain-horizon screening, and an illustrative exosphere particle simulation.

Users can select coordinates, compare sites, explore elevation profiles, adjust simulation parameters, and see how modeled results change over time. The project uses NASA lunar imagery and a terrain dataset derived from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser-altimeter products, alongside calculated ephemeris data.

Lunaris aims to make lunar data and modeling assumptions easier to explore and communicate. It is an educational and early-stage screening tool—not a validated prediction system or a tool for mission, navigation, or safety decisions.
details:
LunarEnvelope's Lunaris is an interactive, open-source screening prototype for comparing lunar locations and dates using NASA-derived data, with every source, assumption and limit stated in the interface and documentation.

WHAT IT DOES. (1) Site Navigator: compare 1 to 3 lunar sites over a 1 to 14 day window between 2020 and 2030. It shows Sun and Earth directions on a local sky plot with a time slider, and reports approximate hours of sunlight, Earth visibility and overlap, with a visibility timeline, a +2 degree clearance sensitivity test, a pinned baseline for comparing runs, and reproducible JSON export. (2) Exosphere Lab: a 3D lunar globe (NASA SVS LROC imagery) where a user picks coordinates, adjusts lunar phase, wind, UV and meteoroid inputs, and sees illustrative exosphere, charging and dust-proxy outputs, a 30-day screening strip, and a comparison with a historical LRO Diviner observation. Selected coordinates carry over between the two views. (3) A seeded ballistic particle pulse (K, He, Na, Ar) integrated in the backend with Newtonian gravity and played back in 3D, a south-polar surface explorer (80 to 90 degrees S map, route elevation profile, exosphere trend chart), and a terrain screen that samples a horizon for one polar site.

HOW IT WORKS. A Python (FastAPI) backend computes the geometry, terrain sampling and models. A TypeScript front end (React, Vite, three.js/WebGL) provides the views. Sun/Earth geometry uses a checksum-verified 2020-2030 table calculated from JPL DE421 / NAIF SPICE kernels, cross-checked against 120 selected archived JPL Horizons cases. Terrain uses a 400 m south-polar grid derived from LRO LOLA. The globe imagery is the NASA SVS LROC colour image.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT. The project makes early site-screening assumptions visible and reproducible for learners and concept-stage explorers: results state their model version, assumptions, dataset hash and limits, and can be exported. Comparisons are meant to show trade-offs between sites, not to rank them.

LIMITATIONS. This is not a validated prediction system and must not be used for mission, equipment, EVA or safety decisions. The comparison uses a spherical Moon and a tangent-plane horizon and omits terrain and antenna constraints. The terrain features cover only 80 to 90 degrees S and use a coarse 400 m grid. The exosphere, charging and dust models use illustrative, unfitted assumptions; the ballistic model is collisionless. The Diviner sample is sparse and historical, not live data. No independent expert review has been done. Passing tests (455 backend tests passed in a local run on 15 November 2026) are regression checks, not physical validation. There is no hosted live demo; run instructions are in the README.

TOOLS. Python, FastAPI, ReportLab, SpiceyPy (ephemeris table generation), TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, lucide-react, Docker recipe (not deployed).

TEAM FACTORS. We prioritised honesty about uncertainty, reproducibility (hashes, pinned sources, exports) and graceful fallbacks (labelled procedural globe if imagery fails, text fallback if WebGL fails).

AI USE. The demo slides and this submission text were prepared with help from Claude (Anthropic).
